<reason>Both sides were sharp and answered pressure questions in the required format, but CON built the cleaner path to victory by narrowing the debate to the marginal dollar and exploiting PRO's own concession that welcoming one more person into an existing building costs "near zero." CON turned PRO's Chicago example against it in the opening and kept that reversal alive through the closing ("the doorbell took care of itself, and hundreds died"). PRO's strongest live points—stacked multi-use returns, the "app routes but never arrives" dependency of CON's volunteers on institutions, and the reminder that most lonely people are mobile (teens, night-shift workers)—were real but never fully resolved the never-visitor problem; PRO's own A1 admitted hours "don't teleport the never-visitor," which CON crystallized as "sensors sense members." CON's minor clipped turn and its somewhat elastic definition of "app-based" (coordination software for outreach) cost it a little, and PRO's retort that the most phone-connected generation is also the loneliest was a fair hit, keeping this competitive rather than lopsided.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 seizing PRO's "near zero" marginal-cost admission [A2.5] and reframing it as "the building is not the binding constraint—fix the pipeline," then following through in Rebuttal 2 and closing when PRO's A1 conceded hours only convert existing visitors into regulars.</best_rebuttal>
